scenario: A systematic review of pharmaceutical trials includes only studies showing a drug effect of at least +15 percentage points improvement over placebo, due to a publication bias toward positive results. A health economist uses the published literature's average effect to estimate true drug efficacy.

data.description: Only trials with measured improvement >= 15pp over placebo are published. Underlying distribution of true drug effects across all conducted trials assumed Normal with known standard deviation Ïƒ = 10 percentage points.

question: The published literature averages a +20pp drug improvement. Using the truncated normal model, estimate (a) the true mean drug effect Î¼ across ALL conducted trials (published and unpublished), and (b) the fraction of conducted trials that appear in the published literature.
naive_answer: The true mean drug effect is approximately +20pp since that is the average in published studies.
naive_trap: Publication bias creates severe truncation. The published +20pp average is the mean of only the top 13% of trials. The true mean effect across all trials is only about +3.7pp â€” the drug is far less effective than the literature suggests.
python_verification:
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.stats import norm
def eq(mu): a=(15-mu)/10; sf=norm.sf(a); return mu+10*norm.pdf(a)/sf-20 if sf>1e-10 else 1e10
mu=brentq(eq,0,14.99)
assert abs(mu-3.69)<0.5
assert abs(norm.sf((15-mu)/10)-0.1290)<0.01
